passage:
[Figure 1]

Percentages of Supplemental Disclosure Filings and Total Penalties Assessed on Importers, by Violation Category, 2019. While most commercial importers entering goods into the European Union submit only a standard customs declaration, trade-policy researchers Christopher Hoffman and Siti Menon note that importers found to have committed certain regulated infractions must additionally submit a supplemental disclosure and remit penalty duties on the affected shipments. Such infractions include "misclassification" (assigning goods to a tariff code that lowers the duty owed), undervaluation of declared shipment worth, and failure to maintain required country-of-origin documentation above a mandated recordkeeping threshold.
prompt: The data in the graph best support which conclusion about supplemental disclosure filings in 2019?

choices.A: Filings involving failure to maintain required country-of-origin documentation must have been associated with higher penalties, on average, than standard customs declarations involving the same infraction.
choices.B: Filings involving misclassification were associated with higher penalties, on average, than filings involving failure to maintain required country-of-origin documentation.
choices.C: Filings involving misclassification and undervaluation collectively accounted for a greater portion of the total penalties than filings involving failure to maintain required country-of-origin documentation.
choices.D: Filings involving failure to maintain required country-of-origin documentation constituted a majority of the filings but accounted for less than a majority of the penalties.

explanation: Choice B is the best answer because the graph supports an average-per-filing comparison. For misclassification, the ratio of the percentage of penalties to the percentage of filings is 42/10, or 4.2. For failure to maintain required country-of-origin documentation, the corresponding ratio is 53/88, or about 0.60. Because 42/10 is greater than 53/88, filings involving misclassification were associated with higher penalties, on average, than filings involving failure to maintain the required documentation.
